In addition to gaining familiarity with debates in these scholarly literatures, students will enhance their research and critical thinking skills by participating in activities such as group discussion questions or analyses of contemporaneous world events. Upon completion of this course, students should be able to understand, critically assess, and convey key debates relating to patterns of global mobility and strategies of migration control as well as apply course learnings to contemporary examples of migration governance and the struggle for mobility rights.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Social Movements
courses.description: The analysis of varieties of social movements and their relationships to social organization and social change.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Migration and Development
courses.description: This course explores theoretical perspectives and empirical studies on development and the related field of migration studies. Specific themes may include history and colonialism, seasonal and labour migration, forced migration, immigration policies and their social and economic implications, and transnationalism and diasporas.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Sociology of Aging
courses.description: An introduction to individual and population aging. Topics discussed include: aging from a historical and comparative perspective; aging in subcultures; aging and the social structure; aging and social processes; aging and the environment; work and retirement; and aging and leisure patterns.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Comparative Health Care Systems
courses.description: This course will examine health care systems around the world from a sociological perspective. Students will utilize health care system evaluation criteria to examine different nations' health care models, including health care delivery and financing. Students will also learn how to apply some introductory research methods for health care systems studies.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Power and Parenting
courses.description: An examination of contemporary parent-child relations in terms of a reconceptualization of power. Special attention will be given to contemporary interpretive (e.g., hermeneutic) approaches to a reformulation of the relation between power and action.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: The Sociology of Community
courses.description: This course examines how our contemporary concern with community is connected with the rise of modern society and the development of the urban-rural debate. Our anxieties about community will be shown to be connected to our anxieties about family. Special attention will be given to the interpretive approach to these issues.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Sociology of Law
courses.description: Through the study of current events in North America, students will examine key theoretical frameworks and questions in the sociology of law. Topics may include the contradictory role law plays in both resolving and exacerbating social inequalities, the persistence of racism, sexism, and other forms of marginalization despite the successes of progressive civil and human rights movements, and controversies surrounding the administration of criminal justice. In examining these questions, students will engage with ideas, arguments, and strategies within socio-legal scholarship and will learn to recognize the strengths and limitations of the law to address social problems.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Studies in Sociology
courses.description: This course will deal with selected topics in sociology. Subjects will be dependent upon the research and/or instructional interests of faculty.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Ethnomethodology in Theory and Practice
courses.description: Ethnomethodology is a study of the methods and practices people use to produce and recognize social actions. Topics may include greetings, the sex/gender distinction, science and common sense, breaching experiments, and jury deliberation.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: The Sociology of Street Gangs
courses.description: This course provides an in-depth exploration into why youth join gangs, their behaviours, and the policy implications that rise out of state and community intervention. Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to a) critically explain the socio-historical development of gangs in the US and Canada; b) explain through criminological and sociological concepts and theories the root causes of gangs and gang violence in contemporary society; and c) understand and articulate the subsequent policy implications. Students will explore these issues through a diverse set of learning strategies including art-based research, group discussions, as well as guest speakers.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: SOC330 (Topic 4: Criminal Gangs)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Criminal Justice Institutions
courses.description: The societal context of policing, courts, and corrections is examined to understand how social control and the law are used in the criminal justice system. Special emphasis is placed on the socio-economic, legal, political, and situational environment that shapes responses to different categories of offenders and offences.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Refugees and Forced Migration
courses.description: In this course students will draw on case studies from past and present to understand why people flee their homes and homelands to seek refuge elsewhere. Students will examine the policies and practices of government and non-governmental agencies in facilitating or blocking such movements. Students will also analyze the attitudes, values, and language that shape local and global responses to refugee movements, on the part of civil society and the state. Students in this course will become acquainted with organizations that work with refugees in the Waterloo Region and will gain a critical understanding of Canada's role in refugee reception.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: PACS301 (Topic 12: Refugees and Forced Migration)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Sociology of Celebrity
courses.description: In this course, students will examine historical and contemporary celebrity through a sociological lens. More specifically, students will apply sociological theory to the study of “traditional” and contemporary social media fame and celebrity. By considering factors such as technological change and capitalism, students will gain a comprehensive understanding of how fame and celebrity have come to occupy a central role in our social lives.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: SOC 330 (Topic 6: Sociology of Celebrity)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: An independent in-depth study of a selected area of concern to the student within the discipline of sociology. Available to individuals or small groups of third- or fourth-year Social Development Studies majors and arranged with one of the faculty members from the program.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: An independent in-depth study of a selected area of concern to the student within the discipline of sociology. Available to individuals or small groups of third or fourth-year Social Development Studies majors and arranged with one of the faculty members from the program.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Theoretical Perspectives on Gender
courses.description: In this course, students will examine sociological theories of gender and gender relations. Students will trace the historical changes in interpretations of gender, with a particular consideration of contemporary theoretical debates. Approaches students will explore include feminist theories as well as political economy and cultural studies.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Religion and Spirituality in the Social and Legal World
courses.description: This course examines key substantive, theoretical, and methodological issues in the field of sociology of religion. Students will critically analyze high-profile media and legal cases surrounding the role of religion, spirituality, and secularity in Canadian society. Students will also further their knowledge by completing their own projects in this thematic area, developing both their research and written skills.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Seminar in Classical Sociological Theory
courses.description: Students will analyze selected original writings by the major figures in the classical sociological tradition of the 19th and early 20th centuries and selected critical literature.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Seminar in Contemporary Sociological Theory
courses.description: Students will analyze selected original writings by influential figures in contemporary theory (i.e., mid-20th century onwards) and selected critical literature.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Contemporary Debates in Sociological Theory
courses.description: Students in this course will examine recent controversies and debates in sociological theory from the 1980s to today. Students will develop a better understanding of contemporary sociological theories and their application.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Health, Surveillance, and Law
courses.description: In this course students will examine how state institutions mobilize public health expertise for regulatory purposes that are instantiated in law and carried out through various forms of social surveillance. With a focus on research in a range of topical fields such as regulatory responses to infectious disease and pandemics, the regulation of people who use drugs, and criminal legal responses to mental health crises, students will apply socio-legal theories to understand and critically evaluate the forms of coercive legal power, intensive surveillance, and formal and informal social control that are authorized in the name of public health.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: LS496 (Topic 23: Health, Surveillance, and Law), SOC430 (Topic 18: Health, Surveillance, and Law)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Surveillance and Society
courses.description: An examination of the way monitoring technologies alter and shape social life in terms of security, fear, control, and vulnerability.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Educational Theory and Practice
courses.description: Students will analyze the major theoretical explanations and practices in education. This analysis will enable students to develop a deeper understanding of the various social processes involved in defining and transmitting knowledge, skills, and power relations from one generation to the next.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Sociology of Higher Education
courses.description: This course examines the relationship between higher education and society. Students will analyze major trends, how and why students are stratified across fields of study and various kinds of post-secondary institutions, and the relationship between education and the labour market.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Culture and Society
courses.description: Students in this course will examine approaches to the study of culture in sociology and related fields. Students will explore debates over the nature of culture, the place of culture in the reproduction of social life, and the role of meaning making in social realms ranging from art, popular culture and the media to politics and morality.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Police Systems and Practices
courses.description: This course examines contemporary issues in policing. Topics may include police response strategies in different models of policing, economics of policing, use of discretion, police accountability, and the changing functions and activities of the police.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Seminar in Social Inequality
courses.description: This course provides students with the tools and vocabulary to understand inequality - how it is produced, how it is experienced and how it is contested in Canada and globally. Students will acquire knowledge about the historic foundations of contemporary inequalities, such as settler colonialism, and will examine proposed technological, political, and institutional solutions that sometimes mitigate inequalities of race, gender, and social class, and sometimes wind up reproducing them instead. Students will deepen their knowledge and expertise of these topics via discussion, research, writing, and class presentations.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Violent Extremism and Terrorism
courses.description: This course examines contemporary issues in terrorism studies. Topics may include the history and comparative analysis of political and religious forms of violent extremism, the process of radicalization and recruitment, the analysis of different forms of terrorist activity, and the counter-terrorism policies and practices.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Peers and Crime
courses.description: This seminar examines the peer influence perspective in criminology. Key theoretical, methodological, and substantive issues and challenges are addressed.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Seminar in Sociology of Health
courses.description: This interdisciplinary course will cover current issues and debates in health, health care, health care systems, and the socio-cultural aspects of population health and well-being. Students will 1) examine health, illness, and health care through a social determinants of health perspective; 2) gain a thorough understanding of the Canadian health care system, especially its strengths and shortcomings with a global perspective; and 3) learn to compare and critically analyze different nations' health care policies.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Crossing Borders: Law and Global Deviance
courses.description: This seminar-style course, positioned at the intersection of sociology and law, examines illicit cross border activity such as terrorism, piracy, drugs, trafficking, and illegal immigration. Each cross-border activity will be examined, along with the way states respond to it politically and legally at a national and international level. Ethnographic research on the activity will provide for rich descriptions of how and why people participate in such activities.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Criminology of Mobility
courses.description: This course offers a critical exploration of the growing nexus of crime control and the control of human mobility under conditions of mass migration and globalization, focusing on the developing area of study called the criminology of mobility (or border criminology). Students will develop an awareness of the social, cultural, and political diversity of law and mechanisms of social control that structure human mobility while paying attention to issues of race, gender, class, and other social relations of power in this field. Students will also develop their oral, written, and digital skills to communicate their ideas about course content through critical assessment of current research.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: LS496 (Topic 7: The Criminology of Mobility), SOC430 (Topic 5: The Criminology of Mobility)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Sentencing as a Social Process
courses.description: This course examines in depth the process and results of criminal sentencing. Topics include types of sentences for criminal and quasi-criminal offences, objectives of sentences, factors affecting sentences, the process of sentencing, the administration and effectiveness of sentences, and unresolved debates in sentencing.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Special Topics in Sociology
courses.description: In this seminar course, students will have the opportunity to learn about a particular topic in the area of sociology or an interdisciplinary field. Students will gain in-depth analysis skills in this selected area of research.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Science as Practice and Culture
courses.description: An examination of science as being constituted by practices which are inevitably social and cultural, as well as of scientific expertise in contemporary issues of new technology, biomedicine, and environmental conflict.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Social Policy Analysis
courses.description: In this interdisciplinary course, students will examine social policy and learn how to conduct policy analysis. Students will develop an understanding of the importance of social policy and evidenced-based policymaking, a familiarity with key concepts in the field of social policy (including social justice, social equity and equality, and distributional issues and stakeholders), and how to effectively apply sociological perspectives and interdisciplinary approaches in policy content analysis. Students will also acquire and apply critical thinking and debate skills in social policy analysis and policy critique, as well as in research-policy translation.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Crime, Law, and Technoscience
courses.description: A critical examination of science and technology in law and criminal justice. Focus will be on topics such as the histories, politics, and cultural representations of forensic sciences and technologies used in evidence collection, surveillance, policing, criminal courts, and incarceration.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Sociology of At-Risk Youth
courses.description: This course examines the social attributes and surrounding conditions associated with at-risk youth. It will focus on the development of youth in three major institutions - education, criminal justice, and mental health care. This course will focus on the attributes of youth themselves, but also on changing institutional definitions and practices. This course may include an experiential learning component outside regular classroom hours.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Cybercrime and Digital Harm
courses.description: An examination of theoretical perspectives and empirical developments surrounding cybercrime, digitally-mediated harms, and associated regulatory responses. A range of topics may be explored, including hacking, technology facilitated abuse, (dis)information, censorship, human rights, and cybersecurity.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: LS496 (Topic 8: Governing Cybercrime), SOC430 (Topic 6: Governing Cybercrime)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Alcohol and Well-Being
courses.description: This seminar examines the relation between well-being, culture, alcohol consumption, and regulation from an interpretive focus. Topics addressed may include health, Alcoholics Anonymous, addiction vs. dependence, prohibition, and social discourses around alcohol consumption.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: SOC430 (Topic 2: Alcohol, Grey Zone, Well-Being)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Computational Social Science
courses.description: The explosion of digital data is revolutionizing the way we learn about the world. This course focuses on the knowledge and skills necessary for doing high-quality social scientific research with digital data. Students will be introduced to the programming language Python, and will learn to collect and analyze digital data using computational methods.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: INTEG475 (Topic 11: "Big Data" and Social Science)
courses.notes: • Previous knowledge of computer programming is not required.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Senior Seminar in Special Topics
courses.description: Senior seminars may include weekly readings, individual and/or group projects, class presentations and discussions, research proposals, essay/literature reviews, assignments, midterms, and final exams. Consult the School of Social, Political and Historical Research listings for topics and prerequisites for the current year.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Humanitarianism
courses.description: This course examines how humanitarianism and its actors shape human displacements and mobilities, marginalized groups, and civil conflicts. Students will learn how to use and apply key concepts related to humanitarianism, and will study their implications for problem solving, developing social policy, and conveying the limits of the field of humanitarianism.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Transnational Organized Crime
courses.description: This seminar course examines contemporary legal regimes surrounding transnational organized crime, terrorism and organized crime, and international money laundering.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Technology and Inequality
courses.description: Students in this course will explore the relationship between technology and inequality - not only in digital and online platforms, but also in the invisible politics of software, hardware, and big data. By focusing on the design and development of technology in recent decades, students will learn how user behaviours and experiences vary across unequal social conditions and experiences in gender, race, class, and global politics. In addition, through the lens of critical design, students will utilize applied methods of critiquing - and even interjecting into - technology's social implications.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: SOC430 (Topic 16: Technology and Society)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Decolonizing Research Through the Urban Arts
courses.description: This course draws on the urban arts to challenge colonial and Eurocentric ways of knowing, including what has become known as the "scientific method". Upon completion of this course, students will be able to a) critically analyze some key limitations of mainstream research methodologies; b) understand the harms that mainstream research methods can at times propagate; c) understand and apply alternative research methods, such as decolonizing arts and urban arts methods; and d) use and apply urban arts in their own research. As part of the course requirements, students will get to explore and create their own artistic expressions.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: LS496 (Topic 29: Urban Arts Research), SOC430 (Topic 22: Urban Arts Research)

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Special Studies
courses.description: An independent, in-depth study, based on empirical research and/or extensive reading in sociology under the direction of individual instructors in sociology. Available to individuals or small groups of Social Development Studies majors and arranged with one of the faculty members from the plan. The project must be approved by the academic supervisor of the course prior to registration.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Honours Research Practicum
courses.description: Denoting a preprofessionalization experience, this course provides selected students with an opportunity to work [to a maximum of 8 hours per week over one term] as an apprentice with a specific instructor on a research project in which the instructor is currently engaged.
courses.notes: • This is a non-paid position and may not be combined with sponsored research positions • Earlier or outside research involvements will not meet the criteria for this course.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Directed Studies
courses.description: Selected study and assignments under the direction of a faculty member.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Senior Honours Essay
courses.description: Directed reading and research in a selected area of sociology inquiry.
courses.notes: • A numeric grade for SOC499A will be submitted only after the completion of SOC499B.

courses.subject: SOC
courses.title: Senior Honours Essay
courses.description: Directed reading and research in a selected area of sociology inquiry.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Introduction to Social Work
courses.description: This course provides an overview of the social work profession and its place in the social welfare system in Canada. Students will examine Indigenous and Eurocentric histories, worldviews, values, and ethics while considering approaches to practice with individuals, families, and communities. Students will learn to think critically about various fields of social work practice as they impact marginalized and disadvantaged social groups.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Social Work with Individuals - Theory and Practice 1
courses.description: Students will be introduced to several theoretical approaches and interventions in the field of social work and begin to develop interview and assessment skills. Students will consider how experiences of oppression and social identities provide the necessary context for understanding the individual in the therapeutic social work relationship.
antireqText: Not completed any of the following: SMF301, SMF311

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Social Work with Groups
courses.description: This course introduces students to the theoretical constructs necessary for an understanding of social work with groups. Students will gain knowledge and develop skills regarding group counselling strategies, effective team functioning, and Indigenous approaches to group work.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Community Organization
courses.description: This course presents students with an overview of different approaches to community organization and community development, and engages students in critical assessment of the theoretical foundations, assumptions, and shortcomings of each approach. Drawing on historical and current examples of social movements and community projects, students will practice analyzing the operations of power, and learn strategies for improving well-being and initiating progressive social change at the community level.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Canadian Social Welfare Policy
courses.description: In this course students will gain an understanding of key concepts in social welfare policy as it has evolved in the post-industrial era and develop their skills in social policy research and analysis. Students will examine various social, economic, and political factors that shape Canadian social welfare policy, critically assess contemporary social policy, discuss policy change processes, and debate current controversies and dilemmas regarding capitalism and the welfare state.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Understanding Diversity in Canada
courses.description: In this course, students will explore diversity of worldviews (e.g., Indigenous, Eurocentric, Eastern) and critically analyze the notion of diversity and inequities in Canada. Students will examine the Eurocentric ideas of "self" and "others," power, privilege, colonization, oppression, discrimination, and intersectionality as they relate to lived experiences of dominance, subjugation, social justice, and social work practice.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Social Work with Families
courses.description: In this course students will learn how political, social, and institutional contexts shape social work practice with families. Students will learn to apply diverse theoretical approaches to working with families, analyze complex situations that social workers and families encounter, and build respectful and anti-oppressive relationships with different family members.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Child Maltreatment: Identification and Prevention
courses.description: The objectives of this course are to provide an understanding of the dimensions and causes of child maltreatment, to develop skills identifying cases of this social problem, and to explore current methods of management and treatment of persons involved in child maltreatment situations.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Developmental Disabilities and Families
courses.description: This course explores the nature and extent of developmental disability in Canada. It reviews traditional approaches to support services and social work practice with people with disabilities and their families, and it examines how these have changed in response to social change movements and milestones. Students consider social work interventions with individuals and families from a strengths-based perspective emphasizing advocacy, empowerment, and social support.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Family Violence
courses.description: An application of the principles and models of medical, psychogenic, and sociogenic adjustment to an understanding of family violence. The treatment of victims of family violence, the prevention of such violence and social policies affecting family welfare are considered.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Social Work in Health Care
courses.description: Analysis of social work in the medical setting, concentrating on identification and treatment of emotional, family, and community aspects of illness. Emphasis is on the concrete application of professional social work to health care, while comparing medical and social work values and concepts of illness.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Studies in Social Work
courses.description: This course will deal with selected topics in social work. Subjects will be dependent upon the research and/or instructional interests of faculty.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: An independent in-depth study of a selected area of concern to the student within the discipline of social work. Available to individuals or small groups of third- or fourth-year Social Development Studies students and arranged with one of the faculty members.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: An independent in-depth study of a selected area of concern to the student within the discipline of social work. Available to individuals or small groups of third- or fourth-year Social Development Studies students and arranged with one of the faculty members.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Senior Seminar in Special Topics
courses.description: Senior seminars may include weekly readings, individual and/or group projects, class presentations and discussions, research proposals, essay/literature reviews, assignments, midterms, and final exams. Consult departmental listings for topics and prerequisites for the current year.

courses.subject: SOCWK
courses.title: Special Studies
courses.description: An independent, in-depth study, based on empirical research and/or extensive reading in social work under the direction of individual instructors in social work. Available to individuals or small groups of Social Development Studies majors and arranged with one of the faculty members from the plan. The project must be approved by the academic supervisor of the course prior to registration.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Introduction to Spanish 1
courses.description: This course is for students with no previous knowledge of Spanish. The basic elements of Spanish grammar will be studied, with emphasis on group and individual oral practice. Focus will be given to the development of skills in listening/comprehension, speaking, reading, and writing. Multimedia exercises accompany each chapter of the textbook. Students will be expected to use them in the multimedia language centre and at home.
antireqText: Not completed: 4U Spanish
Not open to students with native, near-native, or similar advanced ability

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Introduction to Spanish 2
courses.description: This course is a continuation of SPAN101, with emphasis being placed on more advanced elements of Spanish grammar and the spoken language. Students will be provided with a range of opportunities to gain practical insights into the customs and cultural contexts of the contemporary Spanish-speaking world.
antireqText: Not completed: 4U Spanish
Not open to students with native, near-native, or similar advanced ability

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Welcome to Latin America
courses.description: Discover the vibrant diversity of Latin American cultures and societies from their genesis in conquest and colonization through to independence, and the post-colonial quest for identity and self-determination.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Intermediate Spanish 1
courses.description: This course develops intermediate skills in reading, writing, speaking, and listening. The primary goals are to build communicative competence and enhance social and cultural awareness of the Spanish-speaking world.

of.raw: Must have completed the following: 4U Spanish

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Intermediate Spanish 2
courses.description: The course continues development of intermediate skills in reading, writing, speaking, and listening. The primary goals of the course are the further enhancement of communicative competence, and social and cultural awareness. Particular attention is placed on the use of the subjunctive mood.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Spanish Conversation
courses.description: Practice makes perfect! In this course, students will continue to develop and hone their Spanish speaking and listening skills through discussions of current topics in Spanish-speaking countries.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: First Nations, Native Americans, Pueblos Originarios
courses.description: This course will introduce and expose students to the Indigenous civilizations that embody the Americas. Students will look at the cosmogonies, histories, and cultures of Indigenous peoples from pre-Columbian times to the 20th century. They will analyze Latin America's Pueblos Originarios' perspectives on conquest, colonization, and independence, and compare such perspectives to those of First Nations and Native Americans. Through their study of colonial, social, economic, and political relations, students will examine how the meanings of these categories changed over time and how Indigenous peoples have contributed to the ethnically diverse regional societies that continue to characterize Latin America today.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Parallel Revolutions in a Nascent Continent
courses.description: This course provides a broad foundation to the varied and complex geographical, ethnic, social, and historical forces that have shaped contemporary Latin American nations from the early 19th-century independence period to current affairs. Students will be introduced to the diverse regions of the continent: Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, the Bolivarian republics, and the Southern Cone. Students will analyze and discuss nation-building factors such as European-African-Asian-New World interactions, ethnic mixtures, military takeovers, revolutions, U.S. interventions in the region, and migratory experiences. Discussions will also be aimed at contrasting and comparing the contemporary and diverse cultural manifestations of the peoples living in Latin America and the cultural transformation of Latin Americans who have emigrated to other parts of the world, as well as the perceptions of Latin Americans in other cultures.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Approaches to Translation
courses.description: This course introduces students to translation studies through the examination of different approaches to the discipline, along with practical experience. Students review the grammar of the Spanish and English languages within particular contexts as the basis for translation practices. The course also enhances students' lexical and semantic knowledge of the Spanish language through an experiential component in the community.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Spanish in Context 1
courses.description: This course promotes students' oral and written abilities, as well as their critical understanding of Latin American history and culture. Course components include: written and oral/aural practice of Spanish through oral reports, class discussions and debates on assigned topics, short literary works, and films. It offers a review of more advanced grammatical structures with the aim of achieving greater accuracy.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: SPAN261W, SPAN303W

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Spanish in Context 2
courses.description: This course further develops the development of critical understanding of Latin American history and culture. Course components include: assigned readings in a variety of genres, critical cultural analysis, in-class discussions, written essays, and the viewing of films.
antireqText: Not completed nor concurrently enrolled in: SPAN262W, SPAN304W

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Afro-Latin America
courses.description: The African diaspora is central to understanding the historical development and contemporary expressions of Latin American identity. Through the study of historical events, cultural production, and current affairs, this course examines African cultural legacies in Latin America, and explains the economic, societal, and political challenges faced by Afro-Latin Americans today.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Theatre of the Golden Age: Dames, Divas, and Dandies
courses.description: The aim of the course is to acquaint students with works by outstanding playwrights from Spain's Renaissance and Baroque periods. Students will look at the construction of character, the interplay between the sexes, and the struggle for justice.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Lights, Camera, Action! Film Production in Spain and Latin America
courses.description: This course explores how Spanish and Latin American films address the intersection of class, gender, and ethnicity, and the construction of regional, national, and cultural identities.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Special Topics in Hispanic Studies
courses.description: Special topics in Hispanic studies, as announced by the School of Critical and Creative Humanities.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Directed Studies
courses.description: Study in a limited field under tutorial guidance.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Gender, Power, and Representations in Latin America
courses.description: This course analyzes women's cultural production in Latin America. Examining the construction and the representation of gender/sex differences, the course explores the power relations inherent in these representations, while also examining how gender roles and expectations are linked to representations of class, race, sexuality, age, nationality, and ability.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Introduction to Spanish Business Translation
courses.description: This course is designed for students enrolled in their third year of the General or Honours program in Spanish. A strong command of Spanish and English is required. Intense concentration of the Spanish language through oral and written work will focus on business-oriented fundamentals of communication such as letter writing, as well as the translation of primary source materials such as newspapers and business documents.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Cultural Dimensions in English/Spanish Literary Translation
courses.description: This course focuses on the actual practice of translating literature, not only as the transformation of textual expressions, but also as a process of cultural interpretation. Besides reinforcing vocabulary and grammar, students will also review and research notions of different literary genres (poetry, narrative, and theatre), and solidify their knowledge of cultural studies.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Memory, Human Rights, and Reconciliation
courses.description: We remember the past to understand the present and imagine the future. With a focus on Latin America and Spain this course examines how the diverse forms of cultural production help develop our shared understanding of past violations of human rights to demand justice, build resilience, and develop tolerance.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Visual Culture in the Contemporary Hispanic World
courses.description: This course explores the expressive avenues opened up by the confluence of verbal and visual representation in contemporary Hispanic cultural production. Through a close analysis of representative visual and literary works from Latin America and Spain covering a variety of genres and media, including poetry, novel, short story, theatre, painting, photography, and film, the many ways in which words and images interact with each other and make meaning will be examined.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Unruly Women in Early Modern Hispanic Culture
courses.description: This course will examine works by and about women in early modern Hispanic culture (16th and 17th centuries), with particular attention to engagements with and subversions of patriarchal culture in theatre, prose, and poetry. Authors to be discussed may include, among others, Santa Teresa de Avila, Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz, Maria de Zayas, and Ana Caro.
courses.notes: • Taught in English.

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Love in Medieval Spanish Literature (WLU)
courses.description: Taught at Wilfrid Laurier University. Refer to WLU Undergraduate Calendar for course description.

prereq.raw: Must have completed the following: SPAN 223W

courses.subject: SPAN
courses.title: Advanced Translation
courses.description: This course is designed for students enrolled in the third and fourth year of the General or Honours program in Spanish. Fluency in both Spanish and English is required. The objective of this course is to refine translation techniques in order to enable the student to provide accurate and idiomatic translations of English texts in Spanish and vice versa.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Introduction to Sexualities, Relationships, and Families
courses.description: This course introduces students to the study of sexualities, relationships, and families from an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will develop a greater awareness and understanding about healthy relationships that are inclusive of diversity. This course addresses relational violence.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Women, Sex, Marriage, and Family Traditions in Italy
courses.description: This course explores the contributions of Italian women artists, writers, and intellectuals from the Medieval through the Renaissance and Baroque periods. Students will learn about sexual culture, the institution of marriage, the role of the family, and gender roles as portrayed in the works of Italian women from these periods. Students will also assess and compare ideas across these time periods and become aware of the implications of studying these topics in the context of nationality.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Women, Sexual Identities, and Relationships in Italy
courses.description: This course explores the contributions of Italian women artists, writers, and intellectuals from the Enlightenment until contemporary times. Students will assess critically key themes in Italian women’s expression of sexual identities, the nature of relationships, and the influence of family ties as portrayed in Italian literature, art, and philosophy from these periods. Students will become familiar with concepts that mark the development of the Italian female imagery from the 18th to the 21st century.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Special Topics in Sexualities, Relationships, or Families
courses.description: In this course students will engage with diverse materials and approaches in the study of topics on sexualities, relationships, and/or families.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Introduction to Human Sexualities
courses.description: This course provides an interdisciplinary overview of theories and research on human sexualities. Students will explore and deepen their understanding of human sexuality as a complex, diverse, multidimensional, and multilevel domain of life. Students will also learn to critically reflect upon their own understandings and commonly held discourses on human sexualities.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: The Dark Side of Sex and Sexualities
courses.description: Students will engage in the theoretical and empirical examinations of contentious and controversial topics associated with human sexuality. Students may critically examine topics such as sex work, pornography, sexual violence and abuse, incest, compulsive sexual behaviour, and paraphilias.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Parent and Child Relations
courses.description: This course introduces students to parent-child/caregiver-child relationships from a broad interdisciplinary perspective over the lifespan. Students will critically examine topics such as the transition to parenthood, parenting practices and their intersection with child/adult development, social and cultural influences on families with children, gender variance/fluidity and family relationships, and family life challenges.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Introduction to Systemic Therapies and Anti-Oppressive Practices
courses.description: In this course students are introduced to an overview of systemic theoretical and therapeutic practices in relational and sex therapy that apply social justice, anti-oppressive, and inclusionary practices. Students will consider and critically analyze the intersections of social locations such as class, culture, ability/disability, gender, and race within various social contexts. Student learning culminates in the design and presentation of an interactive exhibit project.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Dynamics of Dating
courses.description: This course facilitates students’ knowledge and understanding of the dynamics of intimate relationships in the context of the modern, Western social construct of dating. Topics explored may include digital communications and technology, hook-up culture, long-distance relationships, online dating, polyamorous relationships, and the role of pop culture in dating attitudes and beliefs. Through a variety of assignments and assessments, students will develop a greater awareness of diverse dating processes and structures and critically reflect on their own perspectives about dating.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sexualities and Relationships in Mid/Later Life
courses.description: This course will introduce students to the complexities, tribulations, and joys of navigating sexuality and relationships as humans age. Topics may include physical/biological changes, navigating dementia, youth-focused culture, relationship dissolution and relationship anew, death of partners, family and friends, the menopausal transition, and ageism. Through this course students will increase their understanding of how sexuality and relationships change, grow, and remain the same as people age, and how age intersects with such things as race, gender, sexual orientation, ability/disability, culture, socioeconomic status, and societal expectations, allowing reflection on their own bias, experience, and aging scripts.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sexual Health and Well-Being
courses.description: This course provides students an interdisciplinary overview of sexual health and well-being from a theoretical and practical framework. It unpacks the potential role individuals, communities, and institutions have in defining, preventing, and developing sexual health. Topics may include menstrual equity, STIs and safer sex, chronic and long-term illnesses, 2SLGBTQIA+ sexual health, birth control, and pleasure as health. Students will learn to recognize and challenge potentially harmful normative scripts regarding sexual health and well-being, as well as be given the opportunity to reflect on their own experiences, education, beliefs, and biases in relation to the various dimensions of sexual health.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Constructing Erotics
courses.description: This course examines the social construction of the erotic, in particular how culture, politics, religion, literature, economics, medicine, or technology interact to regulate the definition and performance of sexuality across cultures. Topics may include the sexual body (e.g., beauty and desire), the regulation of sex (e.g., taboos, laws, religion), and other cultural constructions of sexuality (e.g., sexual education).

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sexuality and Popular Culture
courses.description: Students will examine and explore how sex and sexualities are depicted in, shaped by, and contested in popular culture. Students will be introduced to theories in the study of popular culture and sexualities through a range of historical and contemporary texts and practices. Students will be encouraged to recognize and critically reflect on the extent to which human sexualities are complex, intersectional, and multidimensional domains of everyday life as they appear in popular culture forms and how the limits of those forms may shape social understanding of human sexuality.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sexual Pleasure
courses.description: This course provides a theoretical and empirical examination of the pleasurable and recreational aspects of human sexuality. Students will learn about psychological, interpersonal, and sociocultural processes related to discourses, practices, and experiences of sexual pleasure. Students will also learn to critically reflect on various popular and scientific perspectives related to sexual pleasure. Topics may include sexual satisfaction, optimal sexuality, passion, fantasies, eroticism, embodiment, sexual devices and technologies, sexual techniques, BDSM, and sexual role-playing.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sexual Health and Well-Being in Comics
courses.description: This course will present a concentrated history of the major trends and patterns within the representation of human sexuality and sexual health in 20th- and 21st-century comics art. Students will be introduced to the unique and powerful role that comics have played in representing sexuality and sexual well-being through exposure to various artists and scholars on the subject. Students will explore key concepts through close readings of relevant texts, and through the application of key theoretical materials, modelling the kind of analytical work that students will then produce themselves in both discussion and written assignments.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Introduction to Research Methods
courses.description: This course provides an interdisciplinary overview of the philosophical, theoretical, and practical foundations of research methods used in the social sciences and humanities to study sexualities, relationships, and families. Students will learn about both qualitative and quantitative methods, the role of theory in research, and ethical issues pertaining to research. Students will acquire foundational skills for constructing research proposals and becoming critical consumers of research.
antireqText: Not completed any of the following: SWREN251R

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Introduction to Statistics
courses.description: This course introduces the basics of statistics commonly used in the social sciences for the study of sexualities, relationships, and families. Students will learn about the fundamental components, logic, execution, current debates, and best practices related to basic descriptive and inferential statistics. They will learn to read, understand, and interpret statistics, as well as become critical consumers of statistics. They will develop the skills to conduct quantitative analyses using statistical software and write a quantitative research paper.
antireqText: Not completed any of the following: SWREN250R

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Caregiving, Illness, and Relationships
courses.description: In the typical health care model most of the attention is focused on the patient and their well-being, often ignoring the health, financial, and emotional impact on those who provide unpaid informal care and support - family and friends. Through the reading of memoirs, students with an interest in aging, health care, and the therapeutic professions will grapple with the profound impact that caregiving during illness has on carers and relationships across the spectrum - from young carers, to intimate partners, to adult children caring for aging parents, and beyond. Discussions will be grounded in the social, legal, and policy contexts.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Family Policy and the Law
courses.description: There is a persistent tension in our society about where the responsibility for children lies: with the family or the society. This course examines various topics in Canadian social and family policy that affect children's development and family well-being. Topics may include the legislative provisions in areas such as parenting supports, income security, family law, youth justice, caregiving, and the distinct framework for Indigenous families. Students will use foundational concepts and theories to examine the strengths and limitations of policy to address the needs of families.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Communication and Counselling Skills
courses.description: This course introduces students to the theories and methods of communication as applied to processes of individual, relational, and family consultation and counselling. Through functional experiential activities and written reflections, students will apply course concepts and examine their own thoughts, beliefs, and positionings as they develop and strengthen their communication skills. Through application-based course assignments, students will deepen their understanding of intersectional, anti-oppressive frameworks and apply them to active listening and intentional interviewing across human service contexts and relationships.
antireqText: Not completed any of the following: SWREN220R

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Human Sexuality in Relationships
courses.description: This course examines the development and experience of sexuality in a relational context from infancy to old age. Emphasis will be placed on sexual interaction and communication in adult relationships, but the effects of relationships on sexual experiences during infancy, childhood, adolescence, and old age may also be examined.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Social Issues and Controversies in Human Sexuality
courses.description: This course will provide students with an examination of selected issues and controversies in human sexualities, providing an interdisciplinary, learner-centered perspective drawing on family studies, psychology, sociology, feminism, critical scholarship, and more. Through this course students will increase their understanding of the historical, biological, social, political, religious, and cultural forces that shape human sexualities across the lifespan. Students will practice critical thinking and self-reflective skills in the analysis of issues and controversies in the field of human sexuality.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Intimate Relationships
courses.description: Students will examine theories and research to understand the dynamics of interpersonal and intimate relationships. Through examining topics such as attraction, commitment, love, trust, communication, and dissolution, students will expand and deepen their understanding of various theoretical and empirical perspectives about relationships. Students will continue to develop and build on their oral and written capacities to bridge the gap between research, theory, and praxis in understanding and articulating the implications for intimate relationships.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Conflict in Close Relationships
courses.description: Families and close relationships are among the most important and valued human experiences, but they can also be the source of much conflict and pain. Students will build their knowledge as they consider the role that conflict plays in close relationships, with a focus on topics such as family of origin, emotions, power, third-party interventions, breakdown of relationships, conflict styles, and conflict resolution.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Relational Therapy
courses.description: In this course students will learn and engage with modern and postmodern therapeutic approaches to working clinically within relational contexts (e.g., family, romantic, other relationship configurations). This course emphasizes systemic thinking, cultural sensitivity, social justice, and anti-oppressive practices in therapeutic settings. Through experiential assignments/activities students will apply theory to practice and explore ethical implications associated with doing clinical work.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sex Therapy
courses.description: This course will give students the opportunity to critically integrate various therapeutic approaches and clinical issues when working with sexuality-related concerns. Research and theoretical issues in the field of sex therapy will be discussed and applied to clinical contexts. The applied focus enables students to connect clinical theory and ethical issues to practice.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Sexual and Relational Ethics
courses.description: This course provides an interdisciplinary overview of ethics and its applications to sexualities and relationships. Students will learn about basic ethical theories, concepts, issues, and reasoning skills. Students will learn how to apply ethical principles to critically analyze difficult life situations and controversial social issues. Students will learn to engage in and cultivate constructive arguments and discussions on ethical matters.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: History of Sexuality: The Pre-Modern Period
courses.description: This course introduces students to the history of Western sexuality, beginning with the ancient world and focusing primarily on the Middle Ages and the transition to modernity.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: History of Sexuality: The Modern Period
courses.description: This seminar introduces students to the history of sexuality. The course focuses on the 19th and 20th centuries.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Love and the Law
courses.description: Relationship breakdown is a social phenomenon that can have legal consequences. This course provides students with a socio-legal foundation in current family law. Topics may include the court system, the litigation process, property division, spousal and child support, child co-parenting, child protection, high conflict families, and alternative dispute resolution processes. Students will learn about the strengths and limitation of the law to address relationship breakdown and develop transferable skills for careers in policy, social work, mediation, family justice, education, and community service organizations.

of.raw: Earned at least 0.50 units from LS or SRF 200 - 299

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Special Topics in Human Sexualities
courses.description: A specialized course in topics related to human sexualities. Topics cover the application of theory and research in any area related to human sexualities.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Special Topics in Relationships and Families
courses.description: A specialized course in topics that cover the application of theory and research in any area related to relationships and families.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Capstone Seminar
courses.description: This seminar, taken in students’ final Sexualities, Relationships, and Families winter term, invites students to integrate their knowledge in the domains of sexualities, relationships, and families and make connections across academic, experiential, and personal learning throughout their undergraduate education. Students will critically reflect on their learning experiences and how they will apply these to their future endeavours. Students will process their learning through a variety of possible methods, such as reflective writing, presentations, and contributions to a capstone class project.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Independent Study in Sexualities, Relationships, and/or Families
courses.description: Students will develop and write an in-depth study proposal and/or literature review based on empirical research and an extensive reading of a topic in the area of sexualities, relationships, and/or families. Students are generally expected to give a presentation on their project. The project must be approved by the academic supervisor of the course prior to enrolment.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Practicum and Professional Ethics
courses.description: In this course students undertake an unpaid apprenticeship in a human services setting. This practicum field placement is complemented by regular seminar meetings to support and assess student learning. The practicum field placement requires 15 hours per week for eight months (fall and winter terms). Through the practicum experience students learn to integrate and apply their undergraduate Sexualities, Relationships, and Families education and bridge theory, research, and praxis.

of.raw: Earned a minimum major average of 73.0%
An application is required

courses.notes: • SRF490 and SRF491 can be taken independently of the SRF Human Services Practicum Specialization. • The practicum placement component of SRF490 is an eight-month commitment and continues into SRF491; the two courses must be taken in consecutive terms. • Paid or volunteer positions that are obtained outside the context of this course are not eligible for credit in this course.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Practicum and Applied Theory
courses.description: This course is the continuation of the SRF490 practicum field placement along with weekly seminar meetings that focus on integration of theory, practice, and praxis.

of.raw: Earned a minimum major average of 73.0%

courses.notes: • SRF490 and SRF491 can be taken independently of the SRF Human Services Practicum Specialization. • The practicum placement component of SRF491 is a continuation of the placement begun in SRF490; the two courses must be taken in consecutive terms.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Seminar in Sexualities
courses.description: This senior level seminar allows students to further explore, deepen, and integrate their knowledge in the study of sexualities. Students will engage in critical analysis through discussions, presentations, and/or written assignments. Topics reflect current issues from a theoretical and research perspective.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Seminar in the Study of Families
courses.description: This senior level seminar allows students to further explore, deepen, and integrate their knowledge in the domains of relationships and families. Students will engage in critical analysis through discussions, presentations, and written assignments. Topics reflect current issues from a theoretical and research perspective.

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Thesis - Part 1
courses.description: Under supervision of a faculty member, students normally will review literature, design a study, present a research proposal, analyze data, write a scholarly research paper, and deliver an oral presentation based on the paper (e.g., at the SRF Research Symposium).

courses.subject: SRF
courses.title: Thesis - Part 2
courses.description: Continuation of SRF499A.
